2025 OCP Global Summit – "Scale Up" the Key Focus
The AMD Helios rack (ORW), 800 VDC power architecture, Google Deschutes 2MW CDU, and ESUN networking are four major releases at OCP this year. The ongoing efforts remain to scale up and accelerate power-efficient large-scale (gigawatts above) AI data center infrastructure builds in upcoming years.
Key Takeaways
The AMD Helios rack features double-wide of 21" to enable bigger scale-up domains. It is aiming to start shipments in 2H26.
800 VDC solution is in development from solid-state transformer to DC-DC power conversion board, aiming to debut with the Rubin Ultra platform in 2H2027.
Large-scale (>2MW) liquid-to-liquid CDU systems are in focus with upcoming inrow liquid cooling solutions, such as the Google Deschutes CDU.
Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) and CPO switches have been introduced to optimize AI data networking but reliability, serviceability and cost remain key
Major beneficiaries in AP are Wistron and Wiwynn from the AMD Helios rack debut; Delta and BizLink for 800 VDC power solutions; Accton for network upgrade.
The Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit was hosted in San Jose, US on October 13-16. Of the 129 companies (up from 99 last year) ( Exhibit 1 ) that had booths at OCP, 27 were Taiwanese (up from 22 last year) ( Exhibit 2 ). With the continuous increase in compute performance and demand, the key focus areas this year were placed on mechanical, networking (ESUN, CPO, etc), power (800 VDC), and cooling solutions (two-phase cold plates, immersion, etc). Every ODM/OEM showcased their AI server or AI rack solutions, including AMD's (covered by Joseph Moore) newly launched Helios rack architecture and working GB300 trays, which are still air-assisted liquid cooled. Our major takeaways follow.

Major Takeaways from OCP Summit
Scaling up towards larger infrastructure and clusters
In Meta's (covered by Brian Nowak) keynote speech, Vice President, Dan Rabinovitsj, mentioned that Meta has been scaling up its GPU clusters over the past few years, from 128 GPUs to 129K region scale clusters as of last year. It believes it will have to deploy "massive and myriad of clusters" to support its ambitions from here on out ( Exhibit 3 ). Meta is very confident that there is currently not enough compute capacity and that it has line of sight for the next couple of years in terms of the need for all of the compute capacity and demand. Meta said its Richland & Parish site (Hyperion) is just one 5GW datacenter and it is going to build more of these over the next few years ( Exhibit 11 ), and the entire industry is going to build more as well. As a result, the velocity to be able to manufacture and bring up compute capacity will be very critical.
Diversity and mix of different types of hardware
Meta believes that it will continue to have a mixture and diverse portfolio of hardware in its datacenters ( Exhibit 4 ) mainly because: 1) Meta is too big to not have multiple options, so it has resilience and diversity in its supply chain; and 2) it recognizes that sometimes it would find a sweet spot where it can take a certain kind of hardware and deliver a special performance for a particular workload. And it believes these two things will continue to come into play over time, which means scaling on multiple hardware platforms will create significant complexity for the ecosystem. This is why Meta continues to contribute to OCP, to try to drive further standardization, to reduce complexity so that the supply chain would be able to manufacture these supercomputers at a faster pace ( Exhibit 9 ). We believe this echoes what we wrote on Wistron, where we see increased standardization for future Nvidia (covered by Joseph Moore) platforms.
Bigger racks...enabling bigger scale-up domains
This is in an ORW (Open Rack Wide) form factor, which is double the width of the ORV3 rack (21"), which Meta also contributed to OCP. AMD, Meta, and Wiwynn all showcased this rack at their booths. According to Meta, the reason for these bigger racks is to enable larger scale-up domains, because the industry is building silicon that is really dense in FLOPs, and the increase in the number of experts and the need to have these all in a lowlatency environment means that they need to be in the same scale-up domain ( Exhibit 5 ), which means bigger racks. And the only way to do that today, is by having an electrical backplane or midplane, which means the current design has to stay in copper right now, and that is driving the bigger racks. However, there are challenges to building these bigger racks, including: 1) the increased complexity to design and manufacture; 2) they are expensive and heavy to transport; 3) operational challenges, because the serviceability of these bigger racks is more difficult ( Exhibit 7 ). We believe this is something the ecosystem needs to work together on, which is why the industry will need to work and invest together. Meta mentioned that it has never asked its ODM and contract manufacturing partners to invest with it at this scale before, especially since every 10MW of capacity that it delivers in a datacenter, its partners would need to build 1MW of capacity just for testing ( Exhibit 10 ).

Morgan Stanley RESEARCH
However, Meta believes the future has to be disaggregation, so while in the near-term the peak rack power density will continue to increase, it will eventually decline, because the industry will be able to disaggregate using optics ( Exhibit 8 ). Today the industry is tied to the limits of copper in these scale-up domains, but it wants to depend on optics, which would allow for more freedom to drive larger scale-up domains in a larger surface area in the data hall.
AMD Helios to start shipping in 2H26
These Helios racks should start to ship from 2H26, and we believe key customers include Meta, Oracle (press release), and OpenAI, among others. Based on our supply chain checks, Sanmina (SANM.O, not covered) should be the NPI (New Product Introduction) partner for AMD, but Wiwynn should be the main ODM partner for Meta (report link). At the component level, we believe Wistron is the main ODM partner for the GPU mobule, baseboard, as well as the switch tray, which should be positive for the stock, and we believe most PCBs will require M9 grade CCL. This will be a more modular design, with each GPU sitting on its own board, which should help enhance serviceability. These racks can be modular as well, with Meta showcasing its Helios racks with scale-out switches inside the rack, simulating a stand-alone power and super-capacitor rack ( Exhibit 14 ), while AMD showcased its Helios rack with power and super-capacitor shelves inside the rack, simulating a standalone scale-out switch rack ( Exhibit 15 ).
Mechanical component vital in supporting AMD's Helios rack
One key difference in AMD's Helios server rack is the ultra wide form factor (2x that of a ORv3 rack), which will need stronger mechanical components, including chassis and rail kits. We believe this is positive for suppliers like Chenbro and King Slide.
GB300 mass production has begun, while VR200 rack level testing is happening now
Unlike Computex, we actually saw working GB300 compute trays at OCP. From a thermal perspective, the GB300 compute trays that are in mass production today are not fully liquid. It is a hybrid solution (85% liquid / 15% air), with only 6x sets of QD per compute tray ( Exhibit 16 ). GB300 yield rates are not top of mind amongst the people that we conversed with at the booths, which should mean that yields are no longer an issue and production is smooth, especially since most of the rack architecture and components are largely similar to that of GB200. On next-gen VR200, there was limited information at the booths, but we believe the initial rack level production and tests are happening at the moment. These compute trays should be fully liquid-cooled, which means there should 14x sets of QD (vs just 6x sets for GB300), Exhibit 17 .
For VR200, the midplane PCB in the compute tray may be a constraint now, but we still have some time before rack delivery is expected, which should be late 3Q26. Hence, we don't expect imminent impacts on our ODM coverage at this point in time.
Every ODM/OEM that attended OCP showcased their portfolio AI server solutions
For Compal, most of its solutions were 8x GPU solutions, with no GB200 or GB300 solutions. Based on our checks, Compal is able to assemble its AI servers in Taiwan or the US (Texas), but we believe it only has exposure to 8x GPU HGX servers (report link), but contributions are small. For MiTAC (not covered), we also did not see any GB200/300 solutions at its booth. In fact, we did not see any Nvidia HGX systems, only AMD

solutions. Based on our conversations, MiTAC currently only sells 8x AMD GPU solutions. We believe this implies limited competition from MiTAC for Nvidia's standardized products (ie. GB200/300 and 8-GPU HGX systems).
800 VDC solution to drive next generation efficient gigawatt AI factories
As we noted on OCP Day one, 800 VDC allows >150% more power transmitted through the same copper without additional 200-kg copper busbars feeding a single server rack. This improves power usage effectiveness by around 5%, vs. 50V power architecture at conventional data center. The 800 VDC power upgrade takes the cohesive design from data center power facilities, power components to silicon. Delta Electronics at its booth showcased its own-designed solid-state transformer (SST) that features 1.2MW (mass produced already, >3MW in design) in 10-feet cargo container size for mid-voltage fuse and converter, mid-voltage to low-voltage AC/DC, SiC power module and control box. 800 VDC power distribution and protection include 800 VDC eFuse, 90kW DC-DC power shelf and power capacitance shelf and 12kW power distribution board. ( Exhibit 22 ) We expect this to raise power offering value per watt more than double that of the current design, as we highlighted in our data center power and cooling face-off report.
Spec upgrades for power interconnects along with increasing power density
With the increasing power consumption of the AI server clusters, power interconnects will continue to see spec upgrades and dollar content growth. With the advent of stand alone power rack and 800 VDC power rack, power whips and busbars need to come in with more stringent specs (e.g. liquid cooled busbars), which usually means higher ASPs. Moreover, incremental interconnects will be necessary between the power rack and IT rack. We see these as positive dynamics for suppliers like Bizlink.
Google Deschutes CDU introduction unveils in-row liquid cooling solution
Google (covered by Brian Nowak) offers open design for its two megawatt coolant distribution units that features 3 degree Celsius approach temperature difference (ATD), in addition to 80 PSI available pressure to enable advanced cold plate designs for large-scale AI accelerators. BOYD, Cooler Master, Delta Electronics and Envicool are four vendors which showcased the product at their booths. Our check suggests Google consigns VFD (variable frequency drive) from ABB and Delta while consigns water pumps from Speck Pumps in Germany. ( Exhibit 23 ) We also saw MG Cooling (20%-owned by Wistron) presenting its own-design 2.5MW in-row CDU system.
Immersion cooling inflection likely to see inflection in 2028
Promersion presented at OCP, and according to it, immersion cooling, which took a dip in market value this year, will see inflection in 2028 ( Exhibit 19 ). Additionally, Promersion also provided its view of the market share by different cooling technologies, up to 2030 ( Exhibit 18 ), implying cold plate technology will still be the mainstream in the market, which should be a tailwind to cold plate suppliers such as AVC and Auras.
Initiatives to further optimize networking for AI
Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) was introduced by AMD, ARM, Arista,
Broadcom, Cisco, HPE Networking, Marvell, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, OpenAI and Oracle to leverage the mature Ethernet protocol (header, data link layer and PHY layer) to build the high speed, low latency scale up network fabric for AI compute. On the hardware side,

both Accton and Celestica showcased its their latest 1.6T network switch offerings based on Broadcom's (covered by Joseph Moore) Tomahawk 6 ASIC, which we think might start to see early adoption in late 2026 or early 2027. Furthermore, Accton presented a proofof-concept for the CPO switch based on Tomahawk 6 ASIC and its IRIS optical wavelength switch, both representing its efforts to broaden its offerings in different technology architectures.
Data interconnects of growing importance
In the photonics session, Meta unveiled the results of its latest research on co-packaged optics (CPO), which shows that the Tomahawk 5 Bailly 51.2T CPO switch witnessed a annual link failure rate (ALFR) of 0.34% and mean time between failures (MTBF) of 2.6mn hours in the first 15mn device hours of testing, representing better reliability over a comparable pluggable configuration at an ALFR of 1.58% and MTBF of 0.55mn hours. This initial result looks inspiring, though more field testing might be needed for more solid conclusion; meanwhile, serviceability and cost are also key factors for wide CPO adoption in the future. At a higher level, CPO is not just competing against pluggable, but also copper in the data interconnect market, as passive copper still dominates in the scale up network and active copper is gaining share in the scale out network now, as players like TE Connectivity brought forth a actively retimed cable cartridge and Credo/Bizlink, Marvell, etc. showcased their latest 1.6T AEC cables/chips. For demos during OCP, Meta adopted AEC in its GB300 rack and Credo deployed AECs in the Vera Rubin Ultra rack. We remain constructive on the growth opportunities for AEC (active electrical cable) in the coming years as cost effective and reliable solutions compared to its optical counterparts. We expect Bizlink to continue benefiting from this trend.
